UnitStatement: Chapter 6 examines how a licensed professional engineer in Alberta can direct AI agents within Chirality while satisfying EGP Act and APEGA professional obligations.
APEGA's Relying on the Work of Others and Outsourcing standard defines obligations for licensed professionals who rely on work prepared by others.
Direct supervision and control and thorough review obligations are specified in terms of what the licensed professional must do, not what the worker must be.
From the chapter's regulatory standpoint, whether work is prepared by a human subordinate or AI agent is irrelevant to the professional's obligations.
The relevant regulatory question is whether the governance architecture through which the professional directs work satisfies professional obligations in substance.
The chapter argues that Chirality can satisfy direct supervision and thorough review obligations through its governance architecture.
Appendix C provides the full compliance trace from regulatory text to Chirality architectural implementation.
Professional engineering practice in Alberta is governed by the EGP Act and the General Regulation provisions listed in the chapter.
The EGP Act and General Regulation establish conditions for engineering work to be performed, authenticated, and issued for reliance.
APEGA practice standards operationalize legislative requirements for AI-assisted professional practice.
The Relying on the Work of Others and Outsourcing standard defines professional obligations when any portion of a PWP is prepared by others.
The Authenticating Professional Work Products standard governs the final act by which a licensed professional accepts professional responsibility for a PWP.
The PPMP Guideline requires permit holders to document QC/QA processes, including processes for relying on the work of others.
The PPMP defines the firm's practice system within the chapter's regulatory framework.
The relying-on-others standard defines professional obligations when others contribute to PWPs.
The authentication standard defines the act that completes the professional's assumption of responsibility.
The Chirality AI Ltd. professional practice standard documents how licensed professionals satisfy these obligations when using the Chirality agent system.
A professional work product is an output of professional services containing technical information that others rely on for decisions or actions.
In Chirality, PWPs correspond to authenticated deliverables that have reached the ISSUED lifecycle state.
The ISSUED lifecycle state is the final and irreversible state in the deliverable lifecycle state machine.
Agent-produced drafts in IN_PROGRESS or CHECKING states are not PWPs because they have not been accepted by a licensed professional.
A deliverable becomes a PWP only after a licensed professional satisfies direct supervision and control or thorough review and authenticates the work.
Chirality structurally enforces that no agent may advance a deliverable to ISSUED or claim to authenticate work.
The chapter identifies a regulatory gap because APEGA had not issued specific AI-agent or LLM-system guidance as of the writing.
The chapter's AI-assisted practice analysis is an interpretation by the firm and author, not a regulatory determination by APEGA.
Applying existing practice standards to AI-assisted work requires interpretive analysis grounded in regulatory text.
The Relying on the Work of Others and Outsourcing standard does not limit its application to human workers.
The relying-on-others standard defines obligations by what the licensed professional must do, not by the nature or legal status of the worker.
APEGA section 3.0 imposes obligations when a licensed professional relies on work prepared by others.
Direct supervision, review rigor, and documentation duties are specified as obligations of the licensed professional.
The regulatory text does not condition the professional's obligations on the entity's nature, legal status, or professional standing.
The chapter states that the obligations are the same for work prepared by licensed professionals, interns, unlicensed technologists, or supervised contractors.
AI agents directed by a licensed professional assume no professional responsibility.
Responsibility for AI-agent-produced work flows to the licensed professional who authenticates the resulting PWP.
The chapter treats AI-agent work as structurally identical to unlicensed work under direct supervision and control.
The thesis argues that existing APEGA obligations apply directly to AI-assisted professional practice because AI agents are others under section 3.0.
The core regulatory test is whether Chirality satisfies section 3.1.1 direct supervision and section 3.1.2 thorough review in substance.
The chapter and Appendix C answer the regulatory test affirmatively while recognizing the position as interpretive rather than a regulatory ruling.
The AI-agents-as-others argument is the structural foundation of the firm's professional practice standard and this thesis position.
Direct application means the obligations are the same because the regulatory text makes no distinction that would create a different result.
APEGA section 3.1 requires a professional relying on others' work to satisfy direct supervision and control or thorough review before authentication.
Direct supervision and control means directing, monitoring, and controlling engineering work throughout its lifespan, including all engineering decisions.
Thorough review means evaluating outputs sufficiently to verify reliability, validity, and technical accuracy and accept professional responsibility.
Neither direct supervision and control nor thorough review references the nature of the entity that performed the work.
An AI agent that drafts deliverables, extracts dependencies, or returns structured outputs performs work the licensed professional relies on.
A professional must direct AI-agent work through direct-supervision mechanisms or review it through thorough-review mechanisms before authentication.
The chapter identifies an objection that APEGA's others may contemplate natural persons capable of bearing professional responsibility.
The natural-person objection would classify AI agents more like calculation software than subordinate workers.
The chapter flags BC, Ontario, and professional responsibility theory comparisons as unresolved citation targets.

UnitStatement: The firm resolves the tool-versus-worker question conservatively in favor of the others interpretation.
The conservative interpretation imposes the full supervision and review requirements of section 3.1 instead of treating AI outputs as mere tool outputs.
The firm distinguishes tools from workers by the complexity, discretion, and consequentiality of what the system does.
An AI agent interpreting ambiguous documents, proposing decompositions, drafting rationale, and surfacing conflicts exercises a form of judgment without bearing responsibility.
The chapter's regulatory response is to require professionals to supervise and review high-discretion AI outputs with section 3.1 rigor.
The conservative interpretation aligns with APEGA's public-protection purpose through licensed professional accountability.
The LLM technology provider is not providing professional services and does not assume professional responsibility under the EGP Act.
The technology provider supplies a large language model as a technology component within the agent system.
The chapter analogizes the LLM provider to a structural analysis software vendor whose software does not transfer professional responsibility from the engineer.
The firm's agents are the controlled system architecture around the LLM, not the LLM itself.
The agent architecture comprises instruction files, tool access, write scope, governance constraints, and runtime context.
The technology provider supplies the cognitive component, while the firm supplies the governance architecture for professional reliance.
Professional obligations under section 3.1 run to work produced by the governed architecture, not to the LLM's inaccessible internal mechanisms.
The firm must assess the LLM component's capabilities, limitations, failure modes, and model-update impacts on agent behavior.
APEGA section 3.1.1 requires direct supervision and control over work of others.
APEGA section 3.1.1 direct supervision includes active involvement obligations, responsibility-in-decision-making obligations, and PPMP recordkeeping.
Chirality satisfies direct-supervision obligations through architectural mechanisms that are structurally enforced rather than merely procedural recommendations.
APEGA section 3.1.1.1 identifies five active-involvement obligations for direct supervision and control.
The licensed professional directs, monitors, and controls AI-agent work through Chirality's gate-controlled orchestration model.
Type 1 Manager agents operate through interactive sessions where the licensed professional makes consequential decisions at phase transitions.
Type 2 Specialist agents execute only within bounded briefs defined by the licensed professional or an authorized Type 1 agent.
Human authority is the halting condition for every Chirality workflow.
No agent may autonomously advance workflow stages, approve deliverables, or resolve conflicts.
K-GATE-1 and K-SEAL-1 enforce dynamic gates and prohibit Type 2 execution before sealed, gate-approved context.
Authority flows downward and escalation flows upward through the Type 0, Type 1, and Type 2 agent hierarchy.
A Type 2 agent cannot modify Type 0 rules, and a Type 1 agent cannot approve deliverables for external reliance.
The human professional sits above all three agent types in the authority hierarchy.
Every workflow gate requires human authorization before the next stage of work proceeds.
Every agent instruction file declares the agent's type, class, interaction surface, write scope, blocking behavior, outputs, and invariants.
Agent instruction declarations form the documented record of each agent's scope, duties, responsibilities, authorities, and limitations.
K-WRITE-1 guarantees that no agent writes outside its declared zone.
Type 1 agents maintain ongoing communication by presenting structured outputs and awaiting human gate decisions.
Type 2 agents maintain structured communication by receiving INIT-TASK briefs and returning PASS/FAIL run reports with evidence.
Handoff artifacts preserve project context across sessions without hidden state.
Working memory per deliverable is maintained in _MEMORY.md.
In Chirality, every consequential agent output is a versioned artifact in the repository.
AUDIT_AGENTS verifies agent instruction conformance against the canonical standard.
Agent behavior is governed by workflow requirements R1-R9, decomposition invariants I1-I10, and system-wide K invariants.
Instruction files are versioned, reviewed before release, and subject to no silent behavior changes.
The REVIEW agent implements a formal 5-gate review process for lifecycle transitions.
The RECONCILIATION agent performs cross-deliverable coherence analysis.
APEGA section 3.1.1.2 requires the licensed professional to be responsible for all technical engineering decisions.
Every deliverable requires _CONTEXT.md, _DEPENDENCIES.md, and _REFERENCES.md as context files.
Deliverable context files document what the licensed professional considered when directing work.
Technical direction is provided through agent briefs, explicit gate decisions, and human conflict adjudication.
Agents propose and surface conflicts; humans approve and rule.
The gate-controlled workflow makes the licensed professional a required participant in every consequential decision.
Type 2 agents cannot proceed without prior gate approval, and outputs cannot change lifecycle state without human authorization.
Every decision must be recorded in versioned Decision Logs, _MEMORY.md, and _STATUS.md lifecycle history.
K-STATUS-1 designates _STATUS.md as the canonical human-readable lifecycle state file for each deliverable.
Agents are prohibited from maintaining hidden state that diverges from the filesystem.
For reliance purposes, a decision not recorded in a versioned file does not exist.
APEGA section 3.1.1 requires the PPMP to describe direct-supervision processes and associated recordkeeping.
Chirality due-diligence documentation includes agent instruction files, governance documents, git history, and immutable snapshots.
Agent instruction files document scope, duties, authorities, and constraints for each agent.
Governance documents contain the governance framework, design philosophy, specifications, vocabulary, invariants, and architectural design basis.
Git history provides the complete development record of project state, agent outputs, human decisions, and lifecycle transitions.
Immutable snapshots provide a timestamped, append-only audit trail for analysis outputs.
The AI-assisted practice audit trail must allow reconstruction of instructions, outputs, professional review, and gate decisions.
Chirality generates the AI-assisted practice record as an intrinsic byproduct of normal operation.
Thorough review applies to all AI-agent outputs that will be incorporated into PWPs.
Chirality requires thorough review before authentication even when the professional provided direct supervision and control.

UnitStatement: Thorough review audits warrant sufficiency across claims in a deliverable.
During thorough review, the professional examines claims, checks warrants, resolves gaps and conflicts, and determines whether aggregate warrant state supports authentication.
The warrant lifecycle progresses from UNWARRANTED to CITED to REVIEWED to AUTHENTICATED.
The epistemic architecture makes each claim's warrant state visible, enabling targeted review.
APEGA section 3.1.2.1 specifies ten substantive areas that thorough review must address.
The Chirality REVIEW agent structures professional review through a 5-gate protocol.
Gate 1 checks lifecycle state validity and context completeness, with agent validation and human scope confirmation.
Gate 2 derives a review checklist from specifications, decomposition records, and dependencies, with human completeness confirmation.
Gate 3 captures iterative, severity-classified findings.
Gate 4 records human rulings on all findings.
Gate 5 records the lifecycle transition decision, with agent recommendation and human approval.
Deliverable scope, including agent work, is captured in _CONTEXT.md and confirmed at Gate 1.
Risk and operational conditions are captured as governed deliverable content and reviewed through severity-classified findings.
CRITICAL findings must have human-resolved dispositions before a deliverable advances from IN_PROGRESS to CHECKING.
The epistemic labeling framework classifies non-trivial claims as FACT, ASSUMPTION, PROPOSAL, or TBD.
Epistemic labels let a reviewing professional distinguish grounded claims from claims requiring validation.
Suitability for intended purpose and local compliance are confirmed through the Gate 2 checklist.
HSE findings are classified as CRITICAL in the review protocol.
The hierarchy of authority places laws and regulations, including HSE requirements, as the first constraint.
RECONCILIATION performs cross-deliverable coherence analysis across the project dependency graph.
Dependency registers are authoritative deliverable-local records of inter-deliverable relationships with provenance.
Task-level agent outputs are captured in immutable snapshot folders with RUN_SUMMARY.md and QA_Report.md.
Materials and methods are documented within deliverable document kits for datasheets, specifications, guidance, and procedures.
APEGA section 3.1.2.1 treats software, hardware, firmware, applications, and other technologies as tools subject to thorough review.
The licensed professional must understand agent instructions, agent output status, verification methods, and LLM failure modes.
Tasks admitting algorithmic validation are implemented as validated deterministic tools rather than probabilistic LLM reasoning.
Interdisciplinary review obligations are surfaced through Gate 2 when cross-discipline dependencies appear in _DEPENDENCIES.md.
RECONCILIATION identifies interface conflicts across discipline boundaries.
Thorough review must verify compliance with the EGP Act, General Regulation, applicable APEGA standards, and contractual regulatory requirements.
The hierarchy of authority makes laws and regulations the first constraint binding agents and professionals.
Project-specific regulatory requirements are captured in _CONTEXT.md and _REFERENCES.md and appear as mandatory Gate 2 checklist items.
Thorough review must verify compliance with PPMP QC/QA processes and confirm deliverables are clear, readable, consistent, and complete.
Clarity and completeness are structurally enforced through document kits, required metadata files, and the Gate 2 review checklist.
Epistemic labeling ensures assumptions and TBD items are conspicuous rather than hidden in prose.
Authentication is the act by which a licensed professional represents compliance with supervision or review standards and accepts professional responsibility.
Chirality implements authentication as the final and irreversible human action in the deliverable lifecycle.
Authentication binds a professional's seal and signature to a specific git SHA.
Any content change after authentication voids the authentication under K-AUTH-2.
A deliverable is dirty and requires renewed review if governed input changes after its last approved SHA.
Merge to the main branch is permitted only when branch HEAD equals the approved SHA.
SHA-based authentication provides a mechanically verifiable binding between professional approval and approved content.

UnitStatement: Professional obligations addressed by section 6.6 are invariant and cannot be delegated, modified, or bypassed by agents or processes.
Protection of the public, property, and environment is the overriding obligation in professional engineering.
The hierarchy of authority places laws and safety regulations as the first constraint on technical decisions.
When public safety conflicts with commercial pressure, schedule, or convenience, safety prevails.
Public-welfare responsibility is non-delegable to AI systems.
A CRITICAL review finding must be resolved, not deferred, before a deliverable may advance.
Professional liability is personal and non-transferable.
K-AUTH-1 states that only humans author binding approval records.
No agent may claim to certify, approve, sign, seal, or issue work for reliance.
The licensed professional retains decision rights for scope, codes, hazard acceptance, residual risk, conflict adjudication, approval, issuance, signature, seal, and transmittal.
An agent-produced deliverable becomes a PWP only when a licensed professional authenticates it after satisfying supervision or review standards.
The Chirality architecture makes it structurally impossible to skip professional authentication before PWP status.
A licensed professional must not use an AI agent for work they are not competent to verify manually.
Using AI for work the professional cannot adequately review is a competence failure under the EGP Act.
APEGA tool-review obligations imply that professionals must understand agent constraints, output status, verification methods, LLM failure modes, and independent judgment requirements.
Chirality supports competence obligations through epistemic labeling, mandatory provenance, and conflict surfacing.
The architecture cannot substitute for professional competence; it can only make evidence available for competent evaluation.
The firm's practice requires engineering decisions to be based on evidence rather than plausibility.
K-PROV-1 mandates provenance for every extracted claim.
K-INVENT-1 requires unknown values to become TBD rather than guesses.
K-CONFLICT-1 requires conflicts between sources to be surfaced rather than silently resolved.
The epistemic architecture makes the evidence trail the workflow rather than a byproduct of the workflow.
A professional reviewing agent-produced work has direct access to claim evidence, assumptions, and unresolved conflicts.
The technical hierarchy of authority is laws and regulations, codes and standards, approved specifications and design basis, verified analysis and literature, then professional judgment.
Agent outputs carry no professional authority unless accepted and issued by a licensed professional.
The hierarchy of authority is enforced by invariants that prevent agents from overriding codes, standards, or project specifications.
The firm's QC/QA framework for AI-assisted work is implemented through the agent instruction architecture.
Chirality treats quality control as an integral property of agent-governing architecture rather than a separate process overlay.
docs/DIRECTIVE.md provides founding constraints for filesystem-as-state, human authority, evidence-first practice, and no hidden memory.
docs/CONTRACT.md provides binding K invariants with a four-layer enforcement map.
docs/SPEC.md defines physical structures, file formats, and schema validation.
docs/TYPES.md defines controlled vocabulary, enumerated types, and the lifecycle state machine.
agents/AGENT_HELPS_HUMANS.md defines workflow design requirements R1-R9 binding on all agents.
agents/AGENT_DECOMP_BASE.md defines decomposition invariants I1-I10 binding on decomposition agents.
The three-layer invariant system combines workflow requirements, decomposition invariants, and system-wide K invariants.
Chirality verifies compliance at compile time, runtime, human gates, and through automated tooling for selected invariants.
No single point of failure can disable Chirality's entire control system.
Agent instruction files are controlled documents under a release engineering discipline.
Material changes to write scope, tool access, or agent outputs require a recorded release note.
Formal release engineering makes material agent behavior changes visible, reviewed, and documented.
Professionals are informed of agent behavior changes that may affect prior review or supervision validity.
The deterministic and probabilistic boundary is a central QC/QA mechanism.
Tasks that can be validated by schema or algorithm are implemented as deterministic tools instead of LLM reasoning.
LLM-based agents are reserved for inference under uncertainty, including ambiguous interpretation, decompositions, tradeoffs, and drafting.
The deterministic boundary limits the domain of probabilistic outputs requiring thorough review.
The deterministic boundary prevents plausible but incorrect LLM output from replacing verifiably correct deterministic validation.
The firm must evaluate model capabilities and limitations for the professional services it provides.
The firm must assess model safety practices, alignment research, and responsible deployment policies.
The firm must test agent behavior within its instruction architecture before adopting model updates.
The firm must document material model changes and their impact on agent behavior.
The firm does not rely solely on technology-provider safety measures for professional practice compliance.
The agent instruction architecture constrains LLM behavior independently of provider controls.
The professional's tool due-diligence obligation cannot be satisfied by deferring to vendor quality assurance practices.
The evidence and auditability framework rests on filesystem state, git records, immutable snapshots, provenance tracking, and epistemic labeling.
All project truth lives in git-tracked plain files rather than an external database or hidden state.
A decision absent from a versioned file does not exist for reliance purposes.
Version control provides diffs for review, reproducibility, rollback, and audits independent of vendor systems or transient context.
Task-agent analysis outputs are written to timestamped, append-only snapshot folders.
Every extracted claim cites its source file and section reference or carries an explicit location-TBD marker.
All claims are labeled as FACT, ASSUMPTION, PROPOSAL, or TBD.
The evidence trail lets regulators, auditors, or reviewing professionals inspect agent outputs, human decisions, gate transitions, and deliverable versions.
Chirality's audit trail is the normal operational project record rather than a retrospective documentation exercise.
The Human-AI Contract is enforced by the Chirality architecture rather than merely described in policy documents.
Licensed professionals define intent, scope, acceptance criteria, standards, assumptions, and completion criteria.
Agents cannot define their own scope.
Selection of governing codes, standards, and design basis is a human decision right.
Professionals approve changes affecting issued or checked deliverables after being presented downstream implications.
Professionals decide whether independent review beyond the REVIEW agent protocol is required.

AI agents may draft and format deliverables under explicit templates.
AI agents may extract, normalize, cross-reference, and summarize source-document evidence.
AI agents may generate candidate alternatives and tradeoff tables for professional consideration.

Agents prepare information and structure for professional decision-making; they do not make professional decisions.

AI agents are prohibited from bypassing human gates or autonomously advancing workflow stages.

Professional acceptance through supervision or review followed by authentication turns agent outputs into professional work products.

UnitStatement: The structural argument may be more durable than specific regulatory mapping because it rests on professional-conduct obligations in existing text.
The regulatory analysis should be treated as a living document subject to revision as the regulatory context develops.
Chapter 6 establishes that Chirality provides a framework for Alberta licensed engineers to direct AI agents while satisfying EGP Act and APEGA obligations.
The summary restates that AI agents can be interpreted as others under APEGA section 3.0 because obligations are defined by professional conduct.
The summary identifies Chirality as a candidate mechanism for satisfying direct supervision and control through gates, hierarchy, documentation, sessions, records, and audit trails.
The summary identifies Chirality as a candidate mechanism for satisfying thorough review through REVIEW, epistemic labels, SHA authentication, provenance, and conflict surfacing.
Professional obligations that remain invariantly human are enforced as architectural invariants rather than merely recommended in policy.
The chapter's central contribution is that Chirality can serve as a compliance mechanism rather than merely being consistent with regulatory requirements.
Chirality attempts to encode supervision, review infrastructure, and professional prohibitions as system properties.
The chapter's limitations define the scope of the central regulatory-mapping argument rather than defeating it.
The thesis frames Chirality as one defensible way for a licensed professional to direct AI agents under existing APEGA regulation without new AI-specific regulation.
Chapter 7 will assess Chirality through a systems-engineering design-analysis lens.
